name: Malay
confidence_why: Three modern instrumental studies (Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles & Yong 2008; Clynes & Deterding 2011; Wan Aslynn 2012) find no lexical word stress in Standard Malay, only a phrase-final rise-fall that sounds like penultimate stress and moves to the last syllable when the penult is schwa, so the penultimate rule of Winstedt 1913, who himself wrote that no syllable carries a strong accent, describes that phrase-level pattern rather than word stress.
catalog_citation: Winstedt, R.O. 1913. Malay Grammar. Oxford: Clarendon Press. (1st edition; StressTyp2 cites the 1927 2nd edition of the same work.) archive.org id malaygrammar00winsrich.
catalog_quote: § 14. Accent. The need to discuss accent tends to give an exaggerated idea of its importance in Malay. It is necessary to bear in mind that there is no strong accent on any syllable in a Malay word; that words like pĕrkataan, pĕrbuatan, aluran, kĕdĕngaran, di-katakan, for example, are pronounced practically with the same stress on every syllable. Ordinarily in the Malay word, the accent falls on the penultimate except that (1) when the penultimate is ĕ in an open syllable and rarely in a closed, then the accent falls on the last syllable, ĕnám, tĕngáh; (2) when a derivative is built up by prefixes from a monosyllabic root, the accent sometimes remains on that root, namely, on the last syllable; (3) in the vocative, the stress is sometimes thrown on the last syllable. The case of words built up of suffixes presents a special problem. ... The Indonesian rule is that the accent falls on th…
sweep_summary: Six title-keyword items for Standard Malay (five distinct works; Court 1975 appears twice). downloaded and scanned three image-only scans from the SEALang SALA archive (Delilkan 2007 SEALS XIII pp. 25-41; Court 1975 pp. 67-88; Zuraidah Mohd Don 2007 SEALS VIII pp. 65-77, the last via the the Internet Archive because sealang.net went unreachable mid-search), and downloaded the open LOT dissertation Roosman 2006 (LOT 129) as the substitute for the unlocated Roosman 2007 chapter. Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven 2016 stays paywalled (abstract. Radboud handle 2066/168756 could not be reached by automated download). Findings: Delilkan 2007 is a nasal-fusion paper whose only placement claim (penultimate stress possible on a closed schwa penult, impossible on an open schwa penult) is Winstedt 1927 quoted via Hayes 1995 - it confirms but does not independently support the catalog's weight-hedged coding. Court 1975 is about Satun Thai tone assignment to Malay loanwords (Satun Malay one-word statements: final-syllable falling nucleus, high level head) and is silent on Standard Malay stress. Don 2007 is discourse-intonation segmentation, silent on word stress. Roosman (Betawi Malay: no word stress, phrasal accent penultimate medially, final sentence-finally, blocked on schwa) and Maskikit-Essed & Gussenhoven (Ambonese Malay: no stress, no pitch accent) concern other varieties. No new first-hand Standard Malay stress statement was read; the catalog's Winstedt-based coding is unchanged.org APIs and site searches

new_statements.quote: In regard to the vowels a, e, i, o, u, it may be remarked that in open syllables the vowel sound has always a greater degree of intensity than in closed syllables. [...] Similarly in the words bodoh and turut there is more stress on the open syllables bo and tu than on the closed syllables doh and rut; whereas in such words as pada, gigi, jodo and susu there is a heavy stress on both syllables; and so also in such words as panjang, chinchin, pondok, bungkus, where both syllables are closed, the stress is equal in the two syllables, but is much lighter than in open syllables, and the vowel therefore appears to have a shorter sound.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Malay (qs-tier-2026-09-12) carries an empty rule and there are no existing_statements, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict. Shellabear adds a 1904 observation that stress is conditioned by open vs closed syllable rather than by word position, with no culminative word accent, which is broadly compatible with the 'no lexical stress' finding already held by the project in this our files from the earlier search (Clynes & Deterding 2011, JIPA 41(2), printed p. 265: 'There appears to be no inherent lexical stress in the Standard Malay of Brunei'; Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles & Yong 2008, sec. 10: 'there are no phenomena in spoken Malay corresponding to what phonol…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Shellabear gives no positional word-stress rule at all (no mention of penult, final, or accent placement anywhere in the book; the only other hit for 'tone' is 'tone of voice' in the questions lesson). What he calls 'stress' is a property of syllable shape: open syllables carry more vowel intensity than closed ones, so in bodoh/turut the open first syllable is stronger, in pada/gigi/jodo/susu both syllables are 'heavily stressed', and in panjang/pondok/bungkus both syllables are equally and lightly stressed. Stress as described is therefore non-culminative and not a word-level accent; the book is silent on where word stress falls.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the description is by syllable type (open vs closed), not by word position.
new_statements.identity_note: Shellabear describes the Malay of the Straits Settlements / Malay Peninsula (preface signed Malacca, July 1904; American Mission Press romanisation used for Straits vocabularies), i.e. Peninsular Malay a century before the Brunei (Clynes & Deterding 2011) and Peninsular Malaysian (Zuraidah Mohd Don et al. 2008) varieties measured in the sources already held by the project.

tone_statements.citation: Zuraidah Mohd Don, Gerry Knowles & Janet Yong. 2008. How words can be misleading: A study of syllable timing and 'stress' in Malay. The Linguistics Journal 3(2). (HTML article; live URL dead, reached via the Internet Archive 2009-09-10 snapshot.)
tone_statements.quote: Malay has a reputation as a “simple” language, whatever that means. It certainly does not mean it is an easy language to study, and it does not lend itself to generalisations about human language based on English and the languages of Europe. One of its more interesting properties is that it has no stress or tone or any other intermediate level of prosodic organisation. This makes Malay an ideal language to work on for the investigation of prosodic structure. It is certainly a better language for this purpose than English, in which stress and accentuation obfuscate prosodic patterns at discourse level.
tone_statements.locator: Section 10 'Conclusion', sixth (penultimate) paragraph, beginning 'Malay has a reputation as a "simple" language' (HTML article, no page numbers; pp. 66-81)

readall_conflicts: No positional conflict. Shellabear 1904 never states a word-stress position; his 'stress' is open-syllable vowel intensity (both syllables of pada, gigi 'heavily stressed'; both syllables of panjang, pondok equal and light), which cannot be read as penultimate, final, or weight-driven placement in the usual sense (if anything it is the inverse of a heavy-syllable-attracts-stress system, since closed syllables get less). This sits comfortably beside the modern instrumental verdicts already saved in this directory from the earlier search (Clynes & Deterding 2011 'no inherent lexical stress'; Zuraidah Mohd Don, Knowles & Yong 2008 'no phenomena.. corresponding to what phonologists call stress'; Wan Aslynn 2012 'no systematic alignment of both duration and intensity to lexical stress'), which describe no lexical stress and phrase-level prominence only. The one tension is terminological: Shellabear speaks of 'stress' (heavy/light/equal) while the modern sources deny that stress exists as a category; the substance (no culminative word accent) is the same.

tone.quote: Malay has a reputation as a “simple” language, whatever that means. It certainly does not mean it is an easy language to study, and it does not lend itself to generalisations about human language based on English and the languages of Europe. One of its more interesting properties is that it has no stress or tone or any other intermediate level of prosodic organisation. This makes Malay an ideal language to work on for the investigation of prosodic structure. It is certainly a better language for this purpose than English, in which stress and accentuation obfuscate prosodic patterns at discourse level.
tone.locator: Section 10 'Conclusion', sixth (penultimate) paragraph, beginning 'Malay has a reputation as a "simple" language' (HTML article, no page numbers; pp. 66-81)
tone.says: Instrumental study concluding that Malay has no word stress AND no tone: apparent penult stress is the phrase-onset rise plus final cadence of higher-level prosody; explicitly warns against imposing Mandarin-style tone categories or English-style stress categories on Malay prosody.

sources.quote: I refer here to Winstedt's (1927, cited in Hayes 1995b) claim that only an open schwallable in Malay counts as a light syllable. [p. 29] ... This explains why initial stress is possible in a disyllabic root that begins with a closed schwa-headed syllable, but is impossible if the first syllable were an open schwallable. (Winstedt 1927, cited in Hayes 1995b:263). [p. 29, fn. 4] ... I assume further that Malay prosodic words are right-headed and that feet are trochaic, i.e., left-headed (Delilkan 1999 and forward). [p. 26]
sources.note: A theoretical-phonology paper on nasal substitution ('fusion') in Malay prefixation. Stress enters only as assumed metrical structure: trochaic (left-headed) feet inside right-headed prosodic words, head-foot syllables 'bear primary stress' and are ideally closed/heavy (pp. 33-34), 'foot level trochaic stress as well as word level iambic stress' (p. 35). The one concrete placement claim, fn. 4 p. 29, is second-hand: Winstedt 1927 via Hayes 1995 — penultimate (initial in a disyllable) stress is possible when the penult is a closed schwa syllable but impossible when it is an open schwa syllable…

sources.quote: The aim of this paper is to examine the issues of segmentation in continuous discourse and present a theoretical framework that somewhat eases its segmentation into fragmented parts. The difficulty encountered in segmenting a stretch of speech into separate tone groups provides the impetus for carrying out research of this nature. The paper presents arguments for segmenting discourse into units of speech whose boundaries are defined by audible prosodic cues.
sources.note: Discourse-intonation paper: how pause, final-syllable lengthening, pitch change and tempo mark chunk boundaries in spontaneous Malay conversation, with the British-school tone-group model set aside for Malay (p. 66: 'The difficulties encountered when trying to segment Malay discourse using a definition of the nucleus and its domain which was finely tuned for English have led to the abandonment of dividing stretches of speech into tone groups'). The words 'stress'/'unstressed' occur only in the summary of English frameworks (Crystal, O'Connor, Ladd). No statement about Malay word-stress placem…

sources.note: Accent chapter: Malay accent is 'lack of stress' -- both syllables of a stem have nearly the same stress; accent (cued by quantity) lies on the penult except when the penult has schwa, shifting to the new penult under suffixation; sentence accent comparable to French but 'it would be far from the truth to reckon difference of tone under that designation: that is considerable in French, insignificant in Malay' -- i.e. pitch differences play no significant role; the 'singing' tone of Batavian Malay is called a Sundanese practice foreign to genuine Malay. Melodic variation is nowhere treated as…

tone.quote: The accent in a sentence in Malay can be compared with that in French, but then accent means stress or rather, as it is here, lack of stress: it would be far from the truth to reckon difference of tone under that designation : that is considerable in French, insignificant in Malay. I repeat it: Malay speech is dull. The peculiar „singing" tone used by some Batavian natives in speaking Malay is a Sundanese practice, strange to genuine Malay.
tone.locator: chapter 'ACCENT', pp. 98-99; p. 97: 'Malay accent is not to be identified with that in English, Dutch or German. A peculiar feature of it is its lack of stress.. In Malay both syllables of a stem, are pronounced with nearly the same stress.. In a stem the accent lies on the penult, except when this contains [e-breve].'

tone.quote: we propose that intonational variation in Malay can be explained in terms of underlying sequences of abstract tonal units (H and L), which are aligned to the edges and internal syllables of prosodic phrases organized in a hierarchy. [...] We find evidence for at least three levels of prosodic organization: (i) an accentual phrase which comprises one or more words and bears an L and H tone at its left and right edges, respectively, (ii) an intermediate phrase, which serves as the domain of catathesis, and (iii) an intonational phrase, which may span the entire utterance and bears an additional H or L tone at its right edge.
tone.locator: Abstract, p. 106 (see also sec. 3.1 'Accentual Phrase', p. 107: 'we posit that an AP in Malay has a tone sequence of L-H.. where the L tone occurs on its left periphery while the H tone occurs on its right')

sources.note: Intonation in Singapore Malay involves phrase-final rises and an utterance-final rise-fall in declaratives whose location depends on the number of syllables of the final word; acoustic analysis of F0, duration and intensity finds two levels of prosodic phrasing (accentual phrase, intonational phrase) with edge tone(s) at their periphery; focus is marked by a bitonal pitch accent that triggers lowering of post-focus peaks. All tonal events are intonational (AM edge tones / focus accent); no lexical tone.
